screens.title: Chat System — Core Components & Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: We are going to map the core building blocks that make a large-scale chat system reliable and fast. In practice, chat differs from news feeds because it is stateful, bidirectional, and requires persistent connections that survive for long periods. You will learn what roles clients, connection-aware load balancers, WebSocket-based chat servers, message queues, durable storage, presence, user and notification services play. For example, a mobile app opens a single, long-lived WebSocket so the server can push messages with minimal latency. That persistent channel makes connection management, heartbeat handling, and sticky routing essential design concerns. By the end of this lesson you will be able to draw a high-level flow: client → load balancer → chat server → message queue → storage → other chat servers → recipient, and explain why each hop exists. We will also contrast direct messaging with group chat, show where fanout and ordering matter, and call out common mistakes like making servers stateful or ignoring message durability. Think about a chat feature you use daily: the design decisions here explain why messages feel instant and why missed messages are not lost.

Chat System — Core Components & Architecture
Foundations for building scalable, real-time messaging that survives failures and supports many concurrent users.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson

Real-time
Concept Map
Client
Web or mobile app that opens WebSocket and handles reconnection and UI state.
Load Balancer
Connection-aware routing that preserves persistent sessions.
Chat Servers
Maintain WebSockets, publish messages to queue, update presence.
Message Queue
Durable, decoupled delivery for storage and fanout.
Storage
NoSQL stores message history indexed by room and time.
Presence & Notifications
Track online status and push when users are offline.
Explore Key Topics
Three short pivots that ground the chapter.
Persistent connections
Why WebSockets keep latency low and what heartbeats do.
Message durability
Queues and durable storage prevent lost messages on failure.
Presence & fanout
Difference between direct routing and group fanout with many recipients.
Key Takeaway

Design for persistent connections, durable queues, and externalized state so the system can scale horizontally without losing messages.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives will guide how you read the architecture and what decisions matter. First, you should be able to identify the essential components for a scalable chat system: client, connection-aware load balancer, chat servers, message broker, storage, presence, user and notification services. Naming these components helps you partition responsibilities and reason about failure modes. Second, you will understand persistent connections—how WebSockets provide a full-duplex channel and why that changes routing and resource usage compared with HTTP. Third, you will distinguish direct messaging from group chat, noticing how fanout, ordering, and membership management affect scalability. Finally, you will be able to outline the high-level message flow: from the client to chat server to the queue, into storage and to the receiving chat server or notification service. Each objective links a design goal with why it matters to user experience and reliability. By practicing these outcomes you will be better prepared to design a chat architecture that balances latency, durability and operational simplicity.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice and Checks
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond identifying components, practical design skill means explaining trade-offs and spotting common mistakes. You will practice three checks: confirm connection-awareness in your load balancer strategy, ensure message durability via a persistent broker, and verify presence accuracy with a fast in-memory store. For each check we offer a short rationale. Connection-awareness avoids unnecessary reconnections by routing WebSocket traffic consistently. A durable message queue decouples chat servers from slow storage and prevents message loss during spikes. A presence service keeps status queries cheap and avoids overloading chat servers with state. Practice exercises include describing a failure scenario and choosing which component prevents data loss or reconnection storms. These checks build the habit of linking design choices to user-visible outcomes: message latency, delivery guarantees, and online presence accuracy. By rehearsing these checks you reduce the risk of typical pitfalls and improve operational resilience in a chat system.

screens.title: Persistent Connections and WebSockets
screens.narratorSegment: A persistent connection keeps a single network channel open so both client and server can send data whenever needed. The common choice for chat is WebSockets, which run over a single TCP connection and provide full‑duplex messaging. Define this simply: WebSocket is a protocol that upgrades an HTTP connection into a bidirectional channel so servers can push events without client polling. A concrete example is a mobile chat app opening one WebSocket and receiving messages, typing indicators and presence updates over the same connection. This removes the overhead of repeated HTTP handshakes and enables ultra-low latency. One common misconception is that persistent connections always increase server resource use linearly; the reality is that each connection consumes some resources, but efficient server designs and evented input and output let millions of connections be handled with careful tuning and lightweight per-connection state. Heartbeats and reconnection strategies are essential — without them you cannot reliably detect dropped clients. Key practice: measure per-connection memory/descriptor cost and design limits, and provide exponential backoff on reconnect. How would you balance connection limits against user experience in a mobile app?

keyIdea.title: WebSocket in one line
keyIdea.text: A single, long-lived full-duplex TCP channel that reduces latency and enables push-based real-time messaging.

content.html:
Definition
Persistent Connections (WebSocket)
A bidirectional channel that remains open to allow immediate server-to-client and client-to-server messages.
Analogy
Like an open phone call vs repeated voicemails: once open, you can speak instantly without redialing.
Why it matters
  • Enables server push and reduces latency versus polling.
  • Requires connection-aware routing and heartbeat logic.
  • Changes resource planning because connections are long-lived.
Concrete Example
A mobile app opens one WebSocket at login. When user A sends a message, the server pushes it to user B over the existing socket without extra HTTP requests.
Common mistake
Treating connections as free — not planning for file descriptor limits and memory per connection.
Key Takeaway

WebSockets provide the low-latency channel chat needs, but they require careful connection management and efficient server resource use.

screens.title: Connection-aware Load Balancing
screens.narratorSegment: Load balancers are the first hop for client connections and must be configured differently for persistent protocols. Connection-aware or sticky-session routing ensures a client's long-lived WebSocket remains associated with the same backend chat server, preventing needless reconnections. Practically, techniques include IP-hash, consistent hashing, or session affinity mechanisms that remember the original backend. A concrete example: a user establishes a WebSocket through an edge proxy using IP hashing; subsequent messages and heartbeats route to the same server so the server's connection object stays valid. A misconception to avoid is thinking a normal round-robin load balancer is sufficient — with WebSockets it will scatter requests and break existing sessions. Another trade-off is that stickiness can unevenly distribute load, so combine it with connection capacity signals or a shared connection registry. In short, choose a connection-aware strategy, monitor per-backend connection counts, and provide a fallback reconnection plan. Reflect: if a single backend becomes overloaded, what combination of routing and client backoff would you apply to restore stability? Connection-aware Load Balancing means persistent protocols require connection-aware routing so the server-side socket remains consistent for the client.. In practical terms, how sticky routing preserves persistent websocket sessions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Stickiness is essential
keyIdea.text: Persistent protocols require connection-aware routing so the server-side socket remains consistent for the client.

content.html:
Process Flow
Connection-aware Load Balancing
Keep a client's WebSocket tied to the same chat server to preserve the TCP socket and server-side state.
Typical techniques
  • IP hashing or consistent hashing to map clients to backends.
  • Session affinity stored in the load balancer or proxy.
  • Shared routing registry for advanced routing decisions.
Concrete scenario
A chat client uses IP hashing; after a network hiccup it reconnects and lands on the same chat server, preserving its presence and queued messages.
Monitoring and trade-offs
  • Sticky routing can cause hotspots; monitor connection counts per backend.
  • Combine stickiness with capacity-aware routing to rebalance when needed.
  • Provide client-side exponential backoff to avoid reconnect storms when servers fail.
Common mistake
Using a stateless round-robin balancer will break long-lived WebSockets and force clients to reconnect repeatedly.
Key Takeaway

Use connection-aware strategies and monitor backend load to preserve WebSocket sessions and avoid hotspots.

screens.title: Chat Servers — Responsibilities and Scaling
screens.narratorSegment: Chat servers are responsible for accepting WebSocket handshakes, maintaining many persistent connections, receiving client messages, and publishing those messages for delivery and storage. They also manage presence updates and run heartbeat checks to detect dead clients. Architecturally, keep chat servers as stateless as possible: do not persist message history or authoritative presence inside the process. Instead, update external services. This allows horizontal scaling and easier restarts. A concrete example: when a server receives 'Hello' from a client, it tags it with timestamp and sender ID, publishes to the message queue, and updates presence in the presence service. A common misconception is to store active user lists in-memory for fast access; while fast, it makes failover and scaling hard. Instead, store authoritative presence in a distributed in-memory service and cache locally for performance. For capacity planning, measure connections per server, memory per connection, and C P U for message serialization. Finally, plan graceful shutdown procedures to drain connections and migrate presence so users do not lose status or messages. Chat Servers — Responsibilities and Scaling means chat servers should externalize durable state and rely on external presence stores and queues to scale horizontally.. In practical terms, what a websocket server must do at scale. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Chat servers should externalize durable state and rely on external presence stores and queues to scale horizontally.

content.html:
Component
Chat Servers (WebSocket Servers)
Accept connections, relay messages, and update external systems without owning durable state.
Primary responsibilities
  • Handshake and connection lifecycle management.
  • Receive messages, add metadata, and publish to broker.
  • Update presence service and send heartbeats.
Operational practices
Draining connections on shutdown, tracking file descriptor limits, and instrumenting connection counts are essential for stability.
Concrete flow example
Server receives a message, enriches it with timestamp and sender id, publishes to a durable message queue, and notifies interested chat servers to deliver it to recipients.
Common mistake
Embedding message history or authoritative presence inside server memory, which prevents seamless failover and horizontal scaling.
Key Takeaway

Keep chat servers lightweight and externalize durable state so they can be scaled and restarted without loss of messages or presence.

screens.title: Message Queue / Broker
screens.narratorSegment: A message queue or broker is the backbone that decouples producers (chat servers) from consumers (storage services, other chat servers, notification services). When a chat server receives a message, publishing it to a durable broker allows quick acknowledgment to the sender while downstream services process persistence and delivery asynchronously. This solves two core problems: reducing sender latency by offloading heavy work, and providing durability if downstream components fail. For example, when 'Hello' is published to a Kafka topic, a storage consumer reads it and persists to a message database, while chat server consumers forward it to online recipients. A misconception is thinking that a broker alone guarantees single delivery semantics; brokers commonly provide at-least-once delivery, so consumers should handle idempotency and duplicate suppression. Consider partitioning strategies and topic keys to ensure ordering where required, such as using a chat room or conversation ID as the partition key for group chats. Monitoring broker throughput and retention settings determines how long messages remain available for replay and recovery. Message Queue / Broker means use a persistent broker to offload work from chat servers, provide durability and enable multiple independent consumers.. In practical terms, decoupling delivery and ensuring durability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Durable decoupling
keyIdea.text: Use a persistent broker to offload work from chat servers, provide durability and enable multiple independent consumers.

content.html:
Component
Message Queue / Broker
A durable stream where chat servers publish messages and multiple consumers process them independently.
Benefits
Asynchronous processing, durability, replay, and scalable fanout.
Trade-offs
At-least-once semantics require idempotent consumers and careful partitioning for ordering.
Operational notes
Monitor throughput, retention, and consumer lag to avoid message backlog or data loss on failures.
Concrete example
Chat server publishes messages to a topic keyed by conversation ID; storage, notification and delivery services consume independently and process messages in parallel.
Key Takeaway

A durable broker decouples fast acknowledgement from durable persistence and supports multiple downstream processors.

screens.title: Message Storage Service
screens.narratorSegment: Message storage is responsible for durable persistence of chat history and efficient retrieval. Chat systems typically favor NoSQL stores because they provide high write throughput and horizontal scaling for time-series data. Messages are stored keyed by conversation or room ID and indexed by timestamp so clients can fetch recent history or paginate. A concrete example: a consumer reads from the message queue and writes messages to a Cassandra or DynamoDB table with partition key equal to the chat ID and clustering on time. A common misconception is to use a single relational table for all messages; while possible, it often becomes a scalability bottleneck at high write volumes. Consider retention policies and archival for compliance and cost control. Also design efficient read patterns for infinite scroll and gap recovery. Finally, ensure writes are idempotent or use unique message IDs to avoid duplicates when consuming from at-least-once brokers. Message Storage Service means use horizontally scalable nosql for high-throughput message persistence, indexed by conversation and time.. In practical terms, persisting chat history for retrieval and compliance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use horizontally scalable NoSQL for high-throughput message persistence, indexed by conversation and time.

content.html:
Service
Message Storage
Durable persistence of chat messages optimized for write throughput and time-ordered retrieval.
Design patterns
  • Partition by chat room or conversation ID.
  • Cluster by timestamp for efficient recent-history queries.
  • Use retention and archival to manage storage costs.
Concrete example
A consumer writes message records with unique IDs and timestamps to a NoSQL table keyed by conversation ID, enabling efficient pagination and gap recovery.
Common mistake
Using a single centralized relational store without sharding can quickly become a write bottleneck at scale.
Key Takeaway

Choose storage optimized for high write rates and time-ordered queries; plan retention and idempotency for consumer writes.

screens.title: Presence Service
screens.narratorSegment: A presence service records which users are currently online and where they are connected. For low-latency presence checks, systems commonly use an in-memory store like Redis as the authoritative source, while chat servers cache presence for performance. Presence updates occur when users connect, disconnect, or after heartbeat timeouts. A concrete example: when a client connects, the chat server writes a short-lived key into Redis indicating the server id and timestamp. Other services query Redis to display online status. A common misconception is to rely solely on chat server in-memory lists; that breaks when servers restart or when a user’s connection moves between servers. Instead, externalize presence so it survives server restarts and supports cross-server queries. Design details include TTLs for keys to detect stale sessions and compact data shapes that fit in-memory. Also think about presence consistency — eventual consistency is usually acceptable for presence, but stale values should expire quickly to avoid misleading UI. Presence Service means use an external in-memory store to track online status, with ttls and updates from chat servers for accuracy.. In practical terms, tracking online/offline status at scale. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Authoritative presence
keyIdea.text: Use an external in-memory store to track online status, with TTLs and updates from chat servers for accuracy.

content.html:
Component
Presence Service
Fast, in-memory tracking of user online status with TTLs to remove stale entries.
How it works
  • Chat server writes presence entry on connect and deletes on clean disconnect.
  • Heartbeat timeouts remove stale keys via TTL expiration.
  • Other services query presence to show status or route messages.
Concrete example
A Redis key user:123 => {server: cs2, ts: 1660000000} with a 30s TTL indicates current connection location and age.
Common mistake
Keeping presence only in chat server memory so status is lost on restart or unreachable from other servers.
Key Takeaway

Externalize presence to a fast in-memory store with TTLs so status queries remain accurate and resilient to server restarts.

screens.title: Notification Service and Offline Delivery
screens.narratorSegment: Not every recipient is online. A notification service bridges the gap by consuming messages from the broker and sending push notifications or emails as needed. The service consults the presence store; if a user is offline, it formats a push payload and routes it to platform notification gateways. For example, when a message to User B arrives and presence indicates offline, the notification service sends a push and the message remains in durable storage for later retrieval. A common misconception is to assume push replaces storage — it doesn't. Push is a delivery mechanism to notify the user; message history must still be persisted. Also be mindful of rate limits and privacy: only send necessary content in notifications and respect user settings. Operationally, partition notification workloads and monitor failed push attempts for retries. Think about how notification deduplication and batching can reduce noise and cost while ensuring the user learns they have unread messages. Notification Service and Offline Delivery means notification service consumes messages, checks presence, and pushes notifications while storage preserves the full message history.. In practical terms, how messages reach users who are not connected. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Not every recipient is online. A notification service bridges the gap by consuming messages from the broker and sending push notifications or emails as needed. The service consults the presence store; if a user is offline, it formats a push payload and routes it to platform notification gateways. For example, when a message to User B arrives and presence indicates offline, the notification service sends a push and the message remains in durable storage for later retrieval. A common misconception is to assume push replaces storage — it doesn't. Push is a delivery mechanism to notify the user; message history must still be persisted. Also be mindful of rate limits and privacy: only send necessary content in notifications and respect user settings. Operationally, partition notification workloads and monitor failed push attempts for retries. Think about how notification deduplication and batching can reduce noise and cost while ensuring the user learns they have unread messages. Service
Notification Service
Sends push or email when recipients are offline, while preserving messages in storage.
Flow
  1. Consume message from broker.
  2. Check presence store for recipient status.
  3. If offline, send push notification; if online, rely on chat server delivery.
Concrete example
Message arrives, notification service finds recipient offline and sends a push that says 'You have 1 new message' while the full message persists in storage for later fetch.
Common mistake
Relying on push as the single source of truth for delivery; push should complement durable storage, not replace it.
Key Takeaway

Notification services deliver alerts to offline users, but durable storage remains the canonical message record.

screens.title: Direct Messaging vs Group Chat
screens.narratorSegment: Direct messaging is a one-to-one flow with simpler routing: a message needs to be delivered to a single recipient and storage is straightforward. Group chat introduces fanout: one message must be delivered to all active members in a room and persisted so absent members can catch up. Architecturally, direct messages often use point-to-point routing and lightweight presence checks. Group chat benefits from publish-subscribe semantics where servers subscribe to topics that represent rooms and consume only relevant messages. Ordering becomes more important in group chat; using a partitioning key like room ID helps preserve message order per room. Fanout can cause high delivery load: sending a message to thousands of members requires efficient broadcasting strategies and sometimes batching. A common misconception is assuming group chat is just repeated direct messages; in practice, it needs dedicated topic routing, membership management, and care for ordering and backpressure. Consider sharding large rooms and using per-room partitions to maintain order with scalable consumers. One-to-one routing, simple delivery, lower fanout cost.
Group Chat
One-to-many fanout, ordering needs, membership management and higher delivery load.

screens.title: Message Envelope and Processing Example
screens.narratorSegment: A practical way to reason about messages is a small envelope that contains metadata and payload. The envelope typically includes sender id, receiver or room id, timestamp, and a unique message id. When a chat server receives this envelope it should enrich it with server-side metadata, publish it to the broker, and return a quick acknowledgement to the sender. The storage consumer then persists the envelope, and delivery consumers forward it to subscribers. Message Envelope Example
A compact JSON envelope that servers publish to the broker.

screens.title: End-to-End Message Flow (Online & Offline)
screens.narratorSegment: Tracing message flow helps cement where responsibilities lie. Online case: Client A sends 'Hello' over a WebSocket to Chat Server CS1. CS1 enriches the message, publishes to the message queue, and a delivery consumer on CS2 (where Client B is connected) receives the message and forwards it to Client B over its WebSocket. Storage consumers persist the message concurrently. Offline case: CS1 publishes to the broker and the storage consumer persists the message; the notification service consumes and sends a push to Client B based on presence lookup. In both cases the queue provides durability and decoupling. Misconceptions include assuming immediate delivery guarantees — the broker plus storage pattern gives durability but delivery may be asynchronous. Also avoid assuming the same chat server handles both sender and recipient; routing across servers is normal. Consider how acknowledgements are handled at the protocol layer: at-least-once delivery from the broker requires idempotent persistence and clients that can detect duplicates when needed. Which part of the flow would you instrument to diagnose delivery delays? Process
End-to-End Message Flow
A stepwise trace for online and offline recipients.
Online recipient
  1. Client A → WebSocket → CS1
  2. CS1 publishes to Message Queue
  3. CS2 consumes and forwards to Client B over WebSocket
  4. Storage consumer persists message
Offline recipient
  1. Client A → WebSocket → CS1
  2. CS1 publishes to Message Queue
  3. Storage persists the message
  4. Notification service sends push based on presence
Operational check
Instrument queue lag, delivery latency and notification failures. These metrics pinpoint whether delays are in broker processing, storage persistence, or delivery pathways.

Message queues provide the glue between fast acknowledgement and durable persistence; instrument each hop to diagnose delays and failures.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the three most important concepts. First, WebSockets and persistent connections give chat systems their real-time responsiveness but require connection-aware routing and resource planning. Second, decoupling via a durable message queue provides both low sender latency and message durability, allowing storage and notification services to consume independently. fullNarratorScript:
We are going to map the core building blocks that make a large-scale chat system reliable and fast. In practice, chat differs from news feeds because it is stateful, bidirectional, and requires persistent connections that survive for long periods. You will learn what roles clients, connection-aware load balancers, WebSocket-based chat servers, message queues, durable storage, presence, user and notification services play. For example, a mobile app opens a single, long-lived WebSocket so the server can push messages with minimal latency. That persistent channel makes connection management, heartbeat handling, and sticky routing essential design concerns. By the end of this lesson you will be able to draw a high-level flow: client → load balancer → chat server → message queue → storage → other chat servers → recipient, and explain why each hop exists. We will also contrast direct messaging with group chat, show where fanout and ordering matter, and call out common mistakes like making servers stateful or ignoring message durability. Think about a chat feature you use daily: the design decisions here explain why messages feel instant and why missed messages are not lost.

These objectives will guide how you read the architecture and what decisions matter. First, you should be able to identify the essential components for a scalable chat system: client, connection-aware load balancer, chat servers, message broker, storage, presence, user and notification services. Naming these components helps you partition responsibilities and reason about failure modes. Second, you will understand persistent connections—how WebSockets provide a full-duplex channel and why that changes routing and resource usage compared with HTTP. Third, you will distinguish direct messaging from group chat, noticing how fanout, ordering, and membership management affect scalability. Finally, you will be able to outline the high-level message flow: from the client to chat server to the queue, into storage and to the receiving chat server or notification service. Each objective links a design goal with why it matters to user experience and reliability. By practicing these outcomes you will be better prepared to design a chat architecture that balances latency, durability and operational simplicity.

Beyond identifying components, practical design skill means explaining trade-offs and spotting common mistakes. You will practice three checks: confirm connection-awareness in your load balancer strategy, ensure message durability via a persistent broker, and verify presence accuracy with a fast in-memory store. For each check we offer a short rationale. Connection-awareness avoids unnecessary reconnections by routing WebSocket traffic consistently. A durable message queue decouples chat servers from slow storage and prevents message loss during spikes. A presence service keeps status queries cheap and avoids overloading chat servers with state. Practice exercises include describing a failure scenario and choosing which component prevents data loss or reconnection storms. These checks build the habit of linking design choices to user-visible outcomes: message latency, delivery guarantees, and online presence accuracy. By rehearsing these checks you reduce the risk of typical pitfalls and improve operational resilience in a chat system.

A persistent connection keeps a single network channel open so both client and server can send data whenever needed. The common choice for chat is WebSockets, which run over a single TCP connection and provide full‑duplex messaging. Define this simply: WebSocket is a protocol that upgrades an HTTP connection into a bidirectional channel so servers can push events without client polling. A concrete example is a mobile chat app opening one WebSocket and receiving messages, typing indicators and presence updates over the same connection. This removes the overhead of repeated HTTP handshakes and enables ultra-low latency. One common misconception is that persistent connections always increase server resource use linearly; the reality is that each connection consumes some resources, but efficient server designs and evented input and output let millions of connections be handled with careful tuning and lightweight per-connection state. Heartbeats and reconnection strategies are essential — without them you cannot reliably detect dropped clients. Key practice: measure per-connection memory/descriptor cost and design limits, and provide exponential backoff on reconnect. How would you balance connection limits against user experience in a mobile app?

Load balancers are the first hop for client connections and must be configured differently for persistent protocols. Connection-aware or sticky-session routing ensures a client's long-lived WebSocket remains associated with the same backend chat server, preventing needless reconnections. Practically, techniques include IP-hash, consistent hashing, or session affinity mechanisms that remember the original backend. A concrete example: a user establishes a WebSocket through an edge proxy using IP hashing; subsequent messages and heartbeats route to the same server so the server's connection object stays valid. A misconception to avoid is thinking a normal round-robin load balancer is sufficient — with WebSockets it will scatter requests and break existing sessions. Another trade-off is that stickiness can unevenly distribute load, so combine it with connection capacity signals or a shared connection registry. In short, choose a connection-aware strategy, monitor per-backend connection counts, and provide a fallback reconnection plan. Reflect: if a single backend becomes overloaded, what combination of routing and client backoff would you apply to restore stability? Connection-aware Load Balancing means persistent protocols require connection-aware routing so the server-side socket remains consistent for the client.. In practical terms, how sticky routing preserves persistent websocket sessions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Chat servers are responsible for accepting WebSocket handshakes, maintaining many persistent connections, receiving client messages, and publishing those messages for delivery and storage. They also manage presence updates and run heartbeat checks to detect dead clients. Architecturally, keep chat servers as stateless as possible: do not persist message history or authoritative presence inside the process. Instead, update external services. This allows horizontal scaling and easier restarts. A concrete example: when a server receives 'Hello' from a client, it tags it with timestamp and sender ID, publishes to the message queue, and updates presence in the presence service. A common misconception is to store active user lists in-memory for fast access; while fast, it makes failover and scaling hard. Instead, store authoritative presence in a distributed in-memory service and cache locally for performance. For capacity planning, measure connections per server, memory per connection, and C P U for message serialization. Finally, plan graceful shutdown procedures to drain connections and migrate presence so users do not lose status or messages. A message queue or broker is the backbone that decouples producers (chat servers) from consumers (storage services, other chat servers, notification services). When a chat server receives a message, publishing it to a durable broker allows quick acknowledgment to the sender while downstream services process persistence and delivery asynchronously. This solves two core problems: reducing sender latency by offloading heavy work, and providing durability if downstream components fail. For example, when 'Hello' is published to a Kafka topic, a storage consumer reads it and persists to a message database, while chat server consumers forward it to online recipients. A misconception is thinking that a broker alone guarantees single delivery semantics; brokers commonly provide at-least-once delivery, so consumers should handle idempotency and duplicate suppression. Consider partitioning strategies and topic keys to ensure ordering where required, such as using a chat room or conversation ID as the partition key for group chats. Monitoring broker throughput and retention settings determines how long messages remain available for replay and recovery. Message storage is responsible for durable persistence of chat history and efficient retrieval. Chat systems typically favor NoSQL stores because they provide high write throughput and horizontal scaling for time-series data. Messages are stored keyed by conversation or room ID and indexed by timestamp so clients can fetch recent history or paginate. A concrete example: a consumer reads from the message queue and writes messages to a Cassandra or DynamoDB table with partition key equal to the chat ID and clustering on time. Finally, ensure writes are idempotent or use unique message IDs to avoid duplicates when consuming from at-least-once brokers. Tracing message flow helps cement where responsibilities lie. Online case: Client A sends 'Hello' over a WebSocket to Chat Server CS1. CS1 enriches the message, publishes to the message queue, and a delivery consumer on CS2 (where Client B is connected) receives the message and forwards it to Client B over its WebSocket. Storage consumers persist the message concurrently. Offline case: CS1 publishes to the broker and the storage consumer persists the message; the notification service consumes and sends a push to Client B based on presence lookup. In both cases the queue provides durability and decoupling. Let's summarize the three most important concepts. First, WebSockets and persistent connections give chat systems their real-time responsiveness but require connection-aware routing and resource planning. Second, decoupling via a durable message queue provides both low sender latency and message durability, allowing storage and notification services to consume independently. Third, externalize state such as presence and message history. Presence should live in a fast in-memory store with TTLs and message history in a horizontally scalable NoSQL database. Keep chat servers lightweight so you can scale them horizontally, and always design for at-least-once broker semantics by making consumers idempotent.
